gittin-5b-19-20.note: Bar Haddaya wants to carry a divorce document from one country to another and asks how closely he must watch it being written. Rabbi Ahai says he must stand over every letter the scribe writes. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi say it is enough to be present and generally make sure it is done properly. The passage adds that insisting on Ahai's strict way would cast doubt on earlier divorce documents, whose carriers never checked that closely.

people.name: Bar Haddaya
people.about: a man carrying a divorce document between countries

people.name: Rabbi Ahai
people.about: appointed over divorce documents in his location

terms.meaning: The formal document a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.

gittin-5b-19-20.why: The Gemara has been discussing the agent's declaration that a bill of divorce was written and signed in his presence; this case asks how closely he must actually watch the writing to make it.

gittin-5b-21-21.note: Rabba bar bar Chana brought a divorce document half of which was written in his presence and half not. Rabbi Elazar ruled that if the scribe wrote even one line for the woman in his presence, the rest is assumed to be written for her too. Rav Ashi adds that even hearing the sound of the quill and the scroll while it was being written is enough.

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives to end a marriage; it must be written specifically for that woman.

gittin-5b-21-21.why: This continues the question of how much of the writing an agent must witness to declare that a bill of divorce was written in his presence; the teaching cited next is brought as support for Rav Ashi.

gittin-6a-18-18.note: Rav Ḥanin related that Rav Kahana once brought a bill of divorce between Sura and Neharde'a, though he did not know in which direction. Rav Kahana asked Rav whether he had to declare: It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence. Rav said he did not have to, but that if he did, it would help. The Gemara explains: if the husband later came to contest the document, no attention would be paid to him.
gittin-6a-18-18.why: The Gemara is discussing when an agent carrying a bill of divorce must make this declaration, and how Sages required it even for very short distances; this case gives Rav's ruling for travel between two towns in Babylonia.

people.name: Rav Ḥanin
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: The agent who carried the bill of divorce

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who answers Rav Kahana's question

terms.meaning: The get, the document a husband must give his wife to end a Jewish marriage, often delivered by an agent.

terms.term: It was written in my presence and it was signed in my presence
terms.meaning: A declaration an agent bringing a bill of divorce from another place makes, so the document's validity does not need to be proved by witnesses.

gittin-6b-1-3.note: A man bringing a divorce document asks Rabbi Yishmael whether he must say it was written and signed in his presence. Learning he is from the village of Sisai, Rabbi Yishmael tells him he must say it, so the woman will not need witnesses if her husband disputes it. Rabbi Elai objects that Sisai is inside the Land of Israel, where the declaration is not required. Rabbi Yishmael tells him to be quiet: once the divorce was given on the basis of the declaration, it is valid, showing the declaration protects the divorce from later challenge.

people.name: Rabbi Elai
people.about: a student who questions the ruling

people.name: the man from Sisai
people.about: carries the divorce document

terms.meaning: A collection of early rabbinic teachings closely related to the Mishnah.

gittin-6b-1-3.why: The Gemara has just explained that an agent who makes the declaration even when not required means the husband's later challenge is ignored; this incident is cited as the source.

gittin-6b-11-12.note: Rabbi Evyatar asks Elijah the prophet what God is doing, and Elijah says God is studying the story of the concubine in Gibeah and quoting Evyatar's view and Yonatan's differing view. Evyatar wonders why God would mention two opinions if He knows what happened. Elijah answers that both opinions are the words of the living God, and explains how both could be true: the man found a fly in his food and was not upset, but later found a hair and was.

people.name: Yonatan
people.about: holds the other opinion

terms.meaning: A disturbing biblical story from the Book of Judges about a man and his concubine.

gittin-6b-11-12.why: Rabbi Evyatar's standing as a Sage has just been questioned, and Abaye defends him by saying God agreed with his reading; this meeting with Elijah is the proof.

gittin-7a-1-2.note: Rabbi Abbahu teaches that a person should not frighten his household too much, since a great man did and they nearly gave him forbidden food. It was Rabbi Chanina ben Gamliel. The Gemara says he did not actually eat forbidden food: when the animal they brought was missing a limb, his frightened household cut one from a live animal to make it look whole, and he almost ate it.

terms.meaning: A limb cut from a living animal, which the Torah forbids eating.

gittin-7a-1-2.why: The discussion has just quoted Rav that a man who terrifies his household will end up in serious sins, and that household instructions on Shabbat eve must be given calmly. Rabbi Abbahu's account is a concrete case of that danger.

gittin-7a-4-6.note: Mar Ukva, leader of the Jewish community in Babylonia, writes to Rabbi Elazar in the Land of Israel asking whether he may hand over men who torment him to the government. Rabbi Elazar replies only with Bible verses telling him to hold his tongue. When Mar Ukva writes again, Rabbi Elazar tells him to wait patiently for God and to go to the study hall earlier and leave later than his tormentors, and they will disappear on their own. As soon as Rabbi Elazar said this, Geneiva, Mar Ukva's tormentor, was put in a neck iron as a government prisoner.

people.name: Mar Ukva
people.about: the Exilarch, leader of the Jews in Babylonia

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: in the Land of Israel

people.name: Geneiva
people.about: Mar Ukva's tormentor

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, recognized by the government.
Draw lines on parchment before writing, as a scribe does.

gittin-7a-4-6.why: The Gemara has been talking about letters sent from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and the scoring of lines on parchment before writing a verse; Rabbi Elazar's replies are such letters. The next passages pick up the theme of staying silent and leaving judgment to God.

gittin-7a-12-15.note: The Exilarch asks Rav Huna where the ban on placing a garland on a groom's head comes from. Rav Huna cites a mishnah: during Vespasian's war the Sages banned wedding garlands and drums. While Rav Huna steps out, his student Rav Hisda offers a verse (Ezekiel 21:31): when the High Priest's mitre was in place, everyone could wear a garland, and when it is removed, so is the garland. Rav Huna returns and says the ban is rabbinic, but praises Hisda for finding a fine source.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: Rav Huna's student

terms.meaning: The headdress of the High Priest in the Temple.
A rule instituted by the Sages rather than stated in the Torah.

gittin-7a-12-15.why: The discussion has turned to the mourning customs after the Temple's destruction: Mar Ukva has just ruled that song is forbidden. The question of wedding garlands is another such custom, and the verse Rav Ḥisda finds is taken up again in what follows.

gittin-7a-16-16.note: Ravina finds Mar bar Rav Ashi braiding a wedding garland for his daughter and asks if he doesn't follow the rule against garlands derived from the verse about the mitre being removed. Mar bar Rav Ashi answers that the ban applies to men, those comparable to a High Priest. The Sages did not extend it to women, so he may make the garland.

terms.meaning: A rule the Sages enacted as a safeguard or response to events.

gittin-7a-16-16.why: The Gemara has just derived the ban on bridegrooms' garlands from a verse about the High Priest's mitre. This incident marks the limit of that ban: it covers grooms, not brides.

gittin-11b-9-11.note: Rav Huna and Rav Yitzhak bar Yosef discuss whether someone who grabs property for a creditor acquires it for him, while Rabbi Yirmeya dozes nearby. He wakes up and corrects them: if the grab harms other creditors, it does not count. The case of the slave's divorce-from-ownership document is different, because the master said 'give' it, which the Talmud treats like 'acquire it for him'.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: quoted by Rabbi Yirmeya

terms.meaning: A document in which an owner frees his slave.
The earlier collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses.

gittin-11b-9-11.why: The mishna rules that a master cannot take back a bill of freeing a slave once he hands it to an agent. Rav Huna tried to draw a rule about debt collection from that; Rabbi Yirmeya shows why the mishna does not prove it. Rav Ḥisda then links the question to an older dispute.

gittin-14a-8-10.note: Gardeners settled accounts and one was told to give the leftover five coins to the landowner, who formally acquired the money in front of everyone. The gardener later recalculated and found he had no surplus, and asked Rav Nahman for help. Rav Nahman first says he can do nothing, since the landowner already acquired the money. After Rava points out the gardener never said he would not pay a real debt, only that the money was not in his possession, Rav Nahman agrees it was an acquisition made in error, which reverts to the previous owner.

people.name: the gardener
people.about: found no surplus after recalculating

terms.meaning: A formal act that makes a transfer of ownership legally binding.
A unit of money of the time.

gittin-14a-8-10.why: The Gemara has been discussing Rav's rule that a transfer made with all three parties present takes effect at once. Rav Naḥman applies that rule to this case, and Rava's objection shows where it stops: a transfer based on a mistake does not stand.

gittin-14a-16-17.note: Rav Sheshet had cloaks with merchants in Mehoza and asked Rav Yosef bar Hama to bring back the money. The merchants who handed it over wanted a formal act of acquisition so Yosef would be responsible if anything happened to it. Yosef said yes but slipped away without doing it. Rav Sheshet told him he did well, citing the verse 'the borrower is a slave to the lender': either because Yosef avoided binding himself for no reason, or, in another version, because the merchants who owed Sheshet had to see that the money reached him.

people.name: Rav Yosef bar Hama
people.about: sent to collect the money

terms.meaning: A formal act that makes someone legally responsible for an item or sum.

gittin-14a-16-17.why: The Gemara is discussing who bears the risk when money is sent through a messenger, and whether the sender can take it back. This incident shows a messenger avoiding that risk, and Rav Sheshet approving.

gittin-14a-18-18.note: Rabbi Aḥai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya, had a silver vessel in the city of Neharde'a and asked Rabbi Dostai bar Rabbi Yannai and Rabbi Yosei bar Keifar to bring it to him. The people holding it handed it over, then demanded that the two accept formal responsibility for it. When they refused, the people demanded the vessel back. Rabbi Dostai agreed; Rabbi Yosei refused, and the people tormented him. When he appealed to Rabbi Dostai, Rabbi Dostai told them, 'Well done, hit him.' Back home Rabbi Yosei complained to Rabbi Aḥai, who asked Rabbi Dostai why he had done this. Rabbi Dostai described the men: huge, with frightening names, ready to tie up or kill anyone on command. Had they killed him, who would give his father Yannai another son like him? Rabbi Aḥai's reply is not given here.
gittin-14a-18-18.why: The Gemara is discussing who bears the risk when an item is sent through messengers, and whether the senders may retract. Just before, Rav Sheshet's messenger avoided taking on that risk; here two messengers refuse it and the senders try to take the vessel back.

people.name: Rabbi Aḥai
people.about: Son of Rabbi Yoshiya; owner of the silver vessel.

people.name: Rabbi Dostai bar Rabbi Yannai
people.about: One of the two messengers; he gives in to the men and tells them to hit his colleague.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei bar Keifar
people.about: The other messenger, who refuses to return the vessel and is tormented for it.

people.name: Yannai
people.about: Rabbi Dostai's father, named in his defense.

terms.meaning: A formal legal act; here it would have made the messengers responsible for the vessel on the way.

gittin-14b-17-17.note: Rabbi Elazar's colleagues cite a case of a sick woman of the Rokhel family who said to give her brooch, worth 1,200 dinars, to her daughter. After she died, the Sages carried out her wish. Rabbi Elazar curses her sons, meaning it is no proof: they were wicked, so the Sages bent the usual inheritance rules there.

people.name: The sons of Rokhel
people.about: called wicked in the passage

terms.meaning: A coin used as a unit of money.

gittin-14b-17-17.why: The Gemara is explaining a dispute about a dying person who sends money with the word 'deliver.' It ties that to a mishna in which Rabbi Elazar says a dying person's gift needs a formal act, and the Rabbis say words alone suffice. The Rabbis bring this incident as proof; Rabbi Elazar rejects it.

gittin-16b-14-14.note: Rabba bar bar Chana is sick, and Rav Yehuda and Rabba visit him. He answers their question: two people bringing a divorce document from overseas need not say it was written and signed in their presence. Then a Persian priest takes their lamp on a Persian holiday, and Rabba prays to live under either God's shadow or the Romans, not under the Persians.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: from the Land of Israel, per the text

terms.meaning: The document (a get) a husband gives to end a marriage.

gittin-16b-14-14.why: The discussion is about two messengers bringing a bill of divorce from abroad; Rabba bar bar Ḥana's answer bears on that. The lamp episode leads the Gemara to ask whether living under Rome is really better than under Persia.

gittin-18b-6-6.note: A man told ten men to write a divorce document for his wife. Two signed that day and the others up to ten days later. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi ruled that Rabbi Shimon's view, which allows a document written by day and signed at night, can be relied on in urgent circumstances, so once given, the woman is divorced.

terms.meaning: An urgent situation where the rabbis allow a more lenient ruling.

gittin-18b-6-6.why: The Gemara has just set out how Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish differ when a husband asks ten men to sign, including the case of two signing on the day and the rest later. This ruling is that very case, and the Gemara goes on to ask whose view it follows.

gittin-19a-16-16.note: A certain man let witnesses who could not sign their names trace them over a stencil on documents other than a bill of divorce. Rav Kahana had him flogged for it.
gittin-19a-16-16.why: The Gemara has just said that letting witnesses trace their names is allowed only for bills of divorce, so that a woman is not left unable to remarry, and not for financial documents. This case shows that limit enforced.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: The Sage who orders the man flogged.

terms.meaning: Whipped; here a punishment given by the court for breaking a rule of the Sages.

gittin-19b-18-18.note: A man threw what he said was a divorce document into his wife's courtyard among the barrels, but only a mezuza was found there. The question is whether the document was lost and a mezuza happened to be there, or whether he really threw a mezuza and only called it a divorce document. Rav Nahman says a mezuza is rarely kept among barrels, so we assume he threw the mezuza, not a divorce document.

terms.meaning: A small parchment scroll with Torah verses, fixed to a doorpost.
The formal document that ends a marriage.

gittin-19b-18-18.why: The Gemara is asking when a document handed to a wife can be trusted as a bill of divorce, and when the husband can later say it was something else. Here the object itself is in doubt.

gittin-19b-20-20.note: A man took a Torah scroll in the synagogue, gave it to his wife, and said 'This is your bill of divorce.' Rav Yosef considers whether he might have secretly written the divorce on the scroll in invisible gall-water ink. He says that cannot be, since the parchment is itself treated with gall water and a second layer would not last, so there is no concern that a divorce document was written there.

terms.meaning: A liquid used to treat parchment and make ink; here, an invisible way of writing.

gittin-19b-20-20.why: The discussion just before deals with doubtful bills of divorce, and with gall water as a writing liquid. The Gemara goes on to say that Rav Yosef's real point is that rule: gall water does not stay on parchment prepared with gall water.

gittin-27a-4-5.note: A bill of divorce turned up at Rav Huna's court. It named the place as 'Sheviri, the city on the Rakhis River,' and Rav Huna worried there might be two towns called Sheviri, so it might belong to a different couple. Rav Ḥisda told Rabba, then a student, to go and look into it, because Rav Huna would ask him about it that night. Rabba went, examined it, and found a mishna: all documents issued by a court are returned to their owner.
gittin-27a-4-5.why: The Gemara is asking when a lost bill of divorce may be returned. It uses this incident to resolve an apparent contradiction between two rulings of Rabba: the worry about a second person with the same name counts only where two such people are known to exist.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: The Sage whose court the bill of divorce is brought to.

people.name: Rav Ḥisda
people.about: A Sage who sends Rabba to look into the question.

people.name: Rabba
people.about: At this time a student; he finds the source that settles it.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.
The early collection of Jewish law that the Gemara discusses and quotes.

gittin-27b-8-8.note: Rabba bar bar Hana lost a divorce document he was carrying in the study hall, and said he could identify it by a distinguishing mark or by sight. They returned it to him. Afterward he admitted he did not know whether it was returned because of the mark, which Torah law may accept for lost items, or because Torah scholars like him are trusted to recognize an item, which an ordinary man would not be.

terms.meaning: A feature by which an owner can identify a lost item and reclaim it.

gittin-27b-8-8.why: The Gemara has just said that Rav Ashi was unsure whether returning a lost item by its distinguishing marks is Torah law or a rule of the Sages. Rabba bar bar Ḥana's case leaves the same question open.

gittin-29b-8-9.note: A husband sent a divorce document with an agent who did not know the wife, and told him to give it to Abba bar Minyumi, who does. Not finding Abba bar Minyumi, the agent asked three Sages, who said he should hand his agency over to them so they could pass it to Abba bar Minyumi. Rav Safra, sitting with them, objected that the agent was only authorized to hand it to Abba bar Minyumi and cannot pass the role to others. The three Sages were embarrassed that they had ruled wrongly.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: the one who objects

people.name: Abba bar Minyumi
people.about: knows the wife

terms.meaning: Someone appointed to deliver a divorce document for the husband.

gittin-29b-8-9.why: The discussion just before is about when a messenger delivering a bill of divorce may appoint another in his place. Rava and Rav Ashi then argue over whether Rav Safra's objection was right.

gittin-29b-12-16.note: A husband told his agent not to deliver a divorce document until thirty days passed, but circumstances beyond the agent's control meant he could not wait. Rava had him transfer his agency to Rava's court, which would appoint a new agent after thirty days. The Sages challenged this twice, and the second challenge, about the husband changing his mind, seemed to go unanswered; Rava was embarrassed. Then it came out that the woman was only betrothed, not married, and Rava said a man is less likely to change his mind about such a woman, so his ruling was correct.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: quotes a teaching of Rav Huna in Rav's name

terms.meaning: Engaged under a formal betrothal, but not yet fully married.

gittin-29b-12-16.why: Just before, Rav Safra ruled that a messenger never given the power to divorce cannot pass his task on. This case tests that rule on a messenger whose power only starts after thirty days. The Gemara then asks whether the court must appoint a new messenger in the first one's presence.

gittin-30a-1-1.note: A man gave agents a divorce document, saying it would take effect if he had not arrived within thirty days. He reached the river at the end of day thirty, but the ferry was on the far side, so he shouted that he had arrived. Shmuel ruled that this does not count as arriving, even though he clearly meant to, so the divorce document is valid.

terms.meaning: A divorce document that takes effect only if a stated condition is, or is not, met.

gittin-30a-1-1.why: The discussion is about conditional divorces and circumstances outside a person's control. The next case, about a husband who could not appease his wife, is explained by whether such circumstances count in divorce law.

gittin-30a-2-2.note: A man left a divorce document with agents, saying it would take effect if he did not appease his wife within thirty days. He went to appease her, but she was not appeased. Rav Yosef said that he did not truly meet his condition, since he did not even give her a large vessel full of dinars, so the divorce document is valid.

terms.meaning: Win her over so that she is no longer upset with him.

gittin-30a-2-2.why: The Gemara gives a second version of Rav Yosef's ruling in which the divorce does not take effect, and explains the two as a dispute over whether circumstances beyond a person's control count in divorce law.

gittin-31b-9-10.note: Rav Huna and Rav Hisda see Geneiva passing, and one wants to stand for him as a son of the Torah, but the other says he is quarrelsome. Geneiva then asks what they were discussing and they say winds. He passes on a teaching from Rav: four winds blow each day, with the north wind always among them, as the world could not survive without it. The south wind is harshest and would destroy the world were it not held back by the angel Ben Netz.

people.name: Geneiva
people.about: a scholar who passes by

people.name: Rav Hanan bar Rava
people.about: transmits Rav's teaching

terms.meaning: An angel said here to hold back the south wind; the name echoes 'netz' (hawk) in Job 39:26.

gittin-31b-9-10.why: The Gemara has been explaining the harsh east wind of Jonah and how the south wind silences the other winds; this encounter carries the theme of the winds further.

gittin-31b-11-13.note: Rava and Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak see Rav Nahman bar Ya'akov riding past in a gilded carriage with a green cloak. Rava goes to him; Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak first holds back, then also goes when he sees who it is. Rav Nahman bar Ya'akov bares his arm in the heat and names the Shadya wind, and they report Rav, Shmuel and Rabbi Yohanan on its harmful effects on pregnancy and pearls. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak then shows that all three sayings come from one verse in Hosea (13:15).

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Ya'akov
people.about: rides by in the carriage

terms.meaning: The name of a harmful wind in this passage.
The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.

gittin-31b-11-13.why: The Gemara is gathering teachings about winds, after Geneiva's account of the four winds. Right after this, Rava praises Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak as a man of Sura, where they are precise with verses.

gittin-33b-11-11.note: Rabba bar bar Hana recalled that he was one of five elders sitting before Rabbi Yoshiya of Usha. A man came before Rabbi Yoshiya, who compelled him, against his will, to authorize a bill of divorce. Rabbi Yoshiya then told the elders: go and hide, and write the bill of divorce for her.
gittin-33b-11-11.why: The Gemara wants to know which rulings follow Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi and which follow Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel in two disputes about cancelling a bill of divorce. It infers from the order to hide, rather than to scatter, that Rabbi Yoshiya followed one of them in each.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hana
people.about: A Sage who tells this as an eyewitness, one of the five elders present.

people.name: Rabbi Yoshiya from Usha
people.about: The Sage who compels the man to authorize the divorce and tells the elders to hide while writing it.

terms.meaning: The document, called a get, that a husband must have written and delivered to his wife to end a marriage. A husband may try to cancel it before it reaches her.

gittin-34a-2-3.note: Giddul bar Re'ilai sent a divorce document to his wife, but she delayed the messenger by asking him to come back tomorrow. When Giddul heard, he said a blessing thanking God, because he was glad the divorce had not been delivered. The Sages then disagreed: Abaye said his words do not cancel the divorce, while Rava said they do.

people.name: Giddul bar Re’ilai
people.about: the husband

terms.meaning: A messenger the husband sends to hand the divorce document to his wife.
Legally cancelled, so it no longer counts as a valid divorce.

gittin-34a-2-3.why: The Gemara has been discussing how a husband can cancel a bill of divorce he has sent. It explains that Abaye and Rava disagree over whether a husband merely showing that he no longer wants it delivered cancels it.

gittin-34a-5-5.note: Rava points to a case where Rav Sheshet pressed a man to authorize a divorce document against his will. The man then told the witnesses that Rav Sheshet had really said to cancel it. Rav Sheshet made him authorize a new document, which shows he treated the first one as cancelled, even though the man never said so outright.

terms.meaning: The document a husband gives his wife to end a marriage.
Legally cancelled.

gittin-34a-5-5.why: Rava cites this case to prove his view that a husband's showing he does not want the divorce cancels it. Abaye answers that the man had really cancelled it himself, and only blamed Rav Sheshet to avoid being flogged.

gittin-34a-7-7.note: Abaye tells of Rav Yehuda pressing the son-in-law of Rabbi Yirmeya Bira'a to authorize a divorce document. The man cancelled it, twice. The third time Rav Yehuda forced it against his will and had the witnesses put gourd pieces in their ears so they would not hear any cancellation. Abaye argues that if a disclosure of intent mattered in divorce, the document would be void, since the witnesses could see him running after them even without hearing him. So such disclosures must be disregarded.

people.name: Rabbi Yirmeya Bira’a
people.about: the man's father-in-law

terms.meaning: A person's stated private feeling or wish, which the Talmud asks whether it can change a legal act.

gittin-34a-7-7.why: Abaye cites this case to prove that a husband merely showing he does not want the divorce does not cancel it: the witnesses could see him chasing them. Rava replies he might have been running to tell them to hurry.

gittin-34a-11-11.note: A man who was betrothed told witnesses: if I do not marry her within thirty days, let this be a bill of divorce. When the thirty days came, he told them: I tried, but could not. The text does not say what became of the divorce.
gittin-34a-11-11.why: The Gemara asks what doubt there could be: circumstances beyond a man's control do not count for a bill of divorce, and if his words show he no longer wants it, that is the dispute of Abaye and Rava, where the ruling follows Abaye.

terms.meaning: In Talmudic law a couple was first betrothed, which already bound them as husband and wife, and only later married; ending a betrothal required a bill of divorce.
The document, called a get, that ends a marriage or a betrothal. A man could give one on a condition, so that it takes effect only if the condition is not met.

gittin-35a-1-2.note: The Gemara asks why courts stopped making widows take oaths, and considers whether the reason is a story told by Rav Kahana (or, some say, by Rav Yehuda in the name of Rav). During a famine, a man left a gold coin with a widow. Without knowing it, she baked the coin into bread and gave the bread to a poor man. When the owner asked for the coin, she swore that one of her children should be poisoned if she had benefited from it, and soon one of her children died. The Sages concluded that if even a truthful oath is punished this way, a false oath is punished all the more. The Gemara offers this only as a possible reason for the practice.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: one of two possible sources of the story (others say Rav Yehuda, quoting Rav)

terms.meaning: Left with someone for safekeeping, so the keeper must return it.

gittin-35a-1-2.why: The mishna says courts stopped making widows swear an oath to collect their marriage payment. The Gemara asks whether this incident, showing how dangerous an oath is, was the reason, and then asks why it would apply only to widows.

gittin-35a-10-10.note: A widow asked Rav Huna to collect her marriage contract payment from her dead husband's orphaned children. He said he could not help her, because Rav does not let a widow collect it. She replied that the only reason was the concern that she had already taken some of it, and she swore on the spot by the Lord of Hosts that she had not benefited from it at all. Rav Huna ruled that although the court does not make a widow swear, Rav agrees that when she swears of her own accord the oath is accepted, so she can collect.

people.name: Rav
people.about: Rav Huna's teacher, whose ruling he quotes

terms.meaning: A written promise of money the husband owes his wife, due when the marriage ends by divorce or his death.
Here, the dead husband's children, who inherit his property and would have to pay.

gittin-35a-10-10.why: The Gemara has explained that Rav would not let widows collect, because the courts no longer had them swear and vows were taken lightly. Rav Huna's ruling carves out an exception to Rav's practice.

gittin-35a-10-13.note: A widow came before Rav Huna, who said he could not collect her marriage payment because Rav did not; she swore of her own accord that she had taken nothing, and Rav Huna ruled that Rav agrees in such a case. Another widow came before Rav Huna's son, Rabba bar Rav Huna, who told her that neither Rav nor his own father collected a marriage payment for a widow. She asked him at least to give her support. He said she had no right to that either, citing Shmuel: a widow who demands her marriage payment in court loses her support. She said: let his chair be overturned, he has treated me by the rulings of two different people. He overturned his chair and set it up again, and even so he was not spared from weakness.
gittin-35a-10-13.why: The Gemara has explained Rav's refusal to let widows collect their marriage payment. Next, Rav Yehuda, Shmuel's student, tells a judge to find ways to let widows collect, against the practice of Rav's students.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A judge who follows Rav's practice but accepts a widow's oath taken of her own accord; father of Rabba bar Rav Huna.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Rav Huna's son, who refuses a widow both her marriage payment and her support, and is struck by her curse.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage whose ruling, that a widow who sues for her marriage payment loses her support, Rabba bar Rav Huna cites.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, a document promising a wife a sum of money if her husband dies or divorces her; a widow collects it from his estate.
Food and support a widow may draw from her late husband's estate as long as she has not claimed her marriage payment.

gittin-36a-2-2.note: A certain teacher of young children was negligent with them. Rav Aha made him take a vow, with the community's consent, to stop teaching. Later Ravina reinstated him, because no one else could be found who was as careful in teaching as he was.
gittin-36a-2-2.why: Ameimar ruled that a vow taken with the community's consent cannot be released. The Gemara limits this to vows about optional matters: for the sake of a commandment it can be released, as with this teacher.

people.name: Rav Aha
people.about: The Sage who has the negligent teacher vow, with the community's consent, to stop teaching.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The Sage who reinstates the teacher when no equally careful teacher can be found.

terms.term: vow on the consent of the public
terms.meaning: A vow whose terms depend on the community's agreement. Normally a Sage can release a person from a vow, but such a vow was held to be harder to undo.
A commandment or religious duty. Teaching children Torah counts as one.

gittin-37a-10-12.note: A relative of Rabbi Asi held a promissory note with a property guarantee written in it, and asked Rabbi Asi whether the Sabbatical Year cancels it. Rabbi Asi said it does not. The man then went to Rabbi Yoḥanan, who said it does. Rabbi Asi came to Rabbi Yoḥanan and pointed out that Rabbi Yoḥanan himself had said it does not, and that a baraita agreed. Rabbi Yoḥanan answered: because we think so, should we act on it? Perhaps that baraita follows Beit Shammai.
gittin-37a-10-12.why: The Gemara has just reported that Rabbi Yoḥanan and Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish hold the Sabbatical Year does not cancel a note with a property guarantee, with baraitot in support; here Rabbi Yoḥanan refuses to rule that way in practice.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: A Sage whose relative asks about a debt; he challenges Rabbi Yoḥanan

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Rabbi Asi's teacher, who rules that the debt is cancelled

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when by Torah law outstanding debts are cancelled.
A clause in a loan document pledging the borrower's land as security for the debt.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna.
The school of the early Sage Shammai, whose rulings are usually not followed in practice.

gittin-37b-2-3.note: Abba bar Marta brought money to repay Rabba during the Sabbatical Year, when debts are cancelled. Rabba said he cancelled the debt, and Abba took him literally and left with the money. Abaye told him to go back and say he wanted to repay anyway, and then Rabba accepted it. Rabba remarked that this Torah scholar had not known how to respond and had to be taught.

people.name: Abba bar Marta
people.about: also called Abba bar Minyumi

people.name: Rabba
people.about: the lender

people.name: Abaye
people.about: got Abba bar Marta to go back

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when private debts are cancelled.

gittin-37b-2-3.why: The mishna says a lender paid in the Sabbatical Year must say he cancels the debt, but may accept if the borrower says: nevertheless. Rabba has just ruled the lender may hopefully wait for those words, and here he does.

gittin-38a-9-10.note: Shmuel's maidservant was captured and some people redeemed her, then sent her back to him as a maidservant. They claimed even the Rabbis would agree she stayed his. Shmuel did not treat her as a slave and did not even require a document of freedom, since he held she was fully free. The passage says he had already given up hope of getting her back.

terms.meaning: A document that frees a slave.
Giving up hope of recovering something lost, which ends the owner's claim to it.

gittin-38a-9-10.why: The mishna disputes whether a slave ransomed from captivity stays a slave, and the Gemara asks whether that depends on the owner having given up hope. Shmuel acts on his own view that a slave whose owner renounces him is free without a document.

gittin-38a-12-12.note: Rabbi Abba bar Zutra's maidservant was captured, and a non-Jew from Palmyra (a tarmoda'a) redeemed her to be his wife. The Sages sent Rabbi Abba a message that if he wanted to act correctly, he should send her a document of freedom. The text gives only this advice, not the reason or what happened next.

people.name: Rabbi Abba bar Zutra
people.about: the maidservant's owner

terms.meaning: A document that frees a slave.
A word the text applies to the gentile who redeemed her; its exact meaning is not explained here.

gittin-38a-12-12.why: The Gemara asks what a writ of freedom could achieve. It answers that the townspeople would then ransom her as a free Jewish woman, or that her captor would think less of her as a Jew's maidservant and let her be ransomed.

gittin-38a-16-16.note: In Pumbedita, people were having forbidden sexual relations with a certain maidservant, and her master could not stop it. Abaye said he would force the master to free her, so she could marry a Jew and the forbidden conduct would end, except that Rav Yehuda, quoting Shmuel, says freeing a slave breaks a commandment. Ravina replied that in such a case Rav Yehuda would agree that freeing her is allowed, because of the sin others are committing.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: quoted as saying Shmuel's view

terms.meaning: A document that frees a slave.
A commandment to do something, as opposed to a prohibition.

gittin-38a-16-16.why: The Gemara is discussing when a slave may be freed. It goes on to challenge Abaye from a case where a court forced a master to free a half-slave woman, then distinguishes the two.

gittin-38a-16-17.note: In Pumbedita there was a maidservant with whom people were committing forbidden sexual acts. Abaye said that were it not for Shmuel's ruling, reported by Rav Yehuda, that anyone who frees his slave violates a positive commandment, he would force her master to write her a bill of manumission. Ravina said that in a case like this, Rav Yehuda would agree she may be freed, because of the prohibition being violated.
gittin-38a-16-17.why: The Gemara has been discussing when a master sends his maidservant a bill of manumission; after this case it asks whether Abaye truly rejects freeing a slave to stop a sin, citing a half-free woman whose master was forced to free her.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who would force the master to free her if not for Shmuel's ruling

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage who says Rav Yehuda would agree to free her here

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who reports Shmuel's ruling against freeing slaves

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage who ruled that freeing one's slave violates a positive commandment

terms.meaning: A document by which a master frees a slave.
A Torah command to do something, as opposed to a prohibition.

gittin-38b-3-3.note: Rabbi Eliezer went into a synagogue to pray and found only nine men, so he freed his slave to complete the group of ten needed for communal prayer. This is raised as an objection to the idea that freeing a slave is forbidden. The Gemara answers that freeing a slave for a mitzva, like completing a quorum, is a special case, and does not show it is allowed in general.

terms.meaning: The minimum group of ten adult men needed for certain communal prayers.
A teaching from the time of the Mishna that is not in the Mishna itself.

gittin-38b-3-3.why: Shmuel taught that freeing a slave violates a commandment. The Gemara raises Rabbi Eliezer's act as an objection and answers that freeing a slave for the sake of a commandment is different.

gittin-39b-13-14.note: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak found Rava bar She'eilta standing at the door of a house of prayer and asked whether the law follows Rabbi Shimon. Rava bar She'eilta said: I say it does not, but the Sages who came from Mehoza report, in the name of Rav Nahman, that it does. The account goes on: when the speaker came to Sura, he asked Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin what had actually happened. He was told that a maidservant whose master lay dying came crying to him: how long will that woman stay enslaved? The master took his hat, threw it to her, and said: go acquire this, and acquire yourself. When they came before Rav Nahman, he said: he has done nothing.
gittin-39b-13-14.why: Rabbi Shimon holds that a slave is freed only by a writ, not by payment, and the Sages disagree whether the law follows him. Next, the Gemara says Rav Nahman's ruling here did not rest on that view, but on the master having used his own hat for the transfer.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who asks whether the law follows Rabbi Shimon.

people.name: Rava bar She'eilta
people.about: A Sage, found at the door of a house of prayer, who answers and reports what others say.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya bar Avin
people.about: A Sage in Sura who tells what actually happened in the case Rav Nahman ruled on.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The Sage who rules that the dying master's act did not free the maidservant.

terms.meaning: Jewish law as it is actually practised; asking whether the halakha follows a Sage means asking whether his view is the binding one.
A way of transferring ownership by handing over an object; the master tried to give the maidservant ownership of herself by having her take his hat.

gittin-40a-12-12.note: A city of slaves was sold to gentiles, and after their last owners died the slaves asked Ravina to be treated as fully Jewish. He told them to get freedom documents from their first masters' children. The Rabbis objected, citing Ameimar, but Ravina relied on Rav Dimi's report that the heirs can do this. The Gemara concludes the law follows Ravina.

people.name: Rabbi Yochanan
people.about: quoted by Rav Dimi

terms.meaning: A document in which an owner frees his slave.

gittin-40a-12-12.why: The Gemara has just recorded Ameimar and Rav Ashi debating whether a renounced slave can still be freed and whether Rav Dimi's report is mistaken. This case puts that debate into practice, and the Gemara rules like Ravina.

gittin-40a-14-15.note: A slave had two owners, and one freed his half. The other owner feared the court would force him to free his half too, so he gave the slave to his young son, whom the court cannot force. Rav Pappa replied that, since this was a trick, answer it with one: have the slave jingle coins in front of the child so he agrees to free him, and then write the document.

terms.meaning: A document in which an owner frees his slave.

gittin-40a-14-15.why: The Gemara has just ruled, with Ravina, that a bill of manumission can still be written for slaves whose ownership seemed lost; this case shows the Sages finding a way to free a half-freed slave whose owner tried to block it.

gittin-43b-4-4.note: Rav Huna bar Ketina quotes a case where a master was forced to free a woman who was half slave, half free. The Gemara asks whether this follows Rabbi Yochanan ben Beroka, who says women are also commanded to have children. Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak answers no: she was forced to be freed because she could not marry and men were taking liberties with her.

terms.meaning: A woman owned by two masters and freed by only one, so she is partly free.

gittin-43b-4-4.why: The Gemara has been debating what happens to the betrothal of a woman who is half slave and half free when she is freed; this incident shows a court forcing her full freedom, and the Gemara asks on what grounds.

gittin-45a-4-4.note: A slave ran away from outside the Land of Israel into it, and his master followed and came to Rabbi Ami. Rabbi Ami told the master to take a written debt for the slave's value and sign a document freeing him. If he refused, Rabbi Ami said he would take the slave from him entirely, since the slave need not go back outside the Land.

people.name: Rabbi Aḥai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya
people.about: whose statement is the basis

terms.meaning: A document that frees a slave.
A written document recording a debt.
The Land of Israel.

gittin-45a-4-4.why: The Gemara has just discussed why a Jew who buys a slave abroad loses him; this case turns to a slave who flees into the Land of Israel, and the discussion after it explains the verse reading of Rabbi Ahai that Rabbi Ami relied on.

gittin-45a-9-9.note: Rav Hisda's slave ran away to Bei Kutai, a place where Samaritans lived, and Rav Hisda sent asking them to return him. They answered with the verse 'You shall not deliver to his master a slave.' He replied with the verse on lost property: so you shall do with anything your brother has lost. They sent the first verse back again. Rav Hisda answered that it speaks of a slave who fled from outside the Land of Israel into it, as Rabbi Ahai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya, taught. The text does not say whether the slave was returned.
gittin-45a-9-9.why: The Gemara has been collecting rival readings of the verse about not returning a runaway slave; right after, it asks why Rav Hisda chose Rabbi Ahai's reading and answers that this was how the Samaritans themselves understood the verse.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: The master whose slave ran away; he argued by letter with the Samaritans for his return.

people.name: Rabbi Ahai, son of Rabbi Yoshiya
people.about: Sage whose reading of the verse Rav Hisda cited.

terms.meaning: A place where Samaritans lived. Samaritans were a group who accepted the Torah but not the teachings of the Sages.
The Land of Israel.

gittin-45a-11-11.note: Abaye lost a donkey among the Samaritans in Bei Kutai and asked for it back. They asked for a identifying sign, and he said its belly was white. They answered that this is not a real sign, since all donkeys have white bellies, but they would send it only because they knew Abaye was trustworthy.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: also called Naḥmani in the text

terms.meaning: A detail that proves a lost item is really yours.
A place where Samaritans lived.

gittin-45a-11-11.why: It comes right after Rav Hisda's exchange with the same Samaritans of Bei Kutai over his runaway slave, which turned on the verse about returning a brother's lost property.

gittin-45a-17-21.note: Rav Naḥman's daughters could stir a boiling pot with bare hands, and were taken captive, along with Rav Ilish, because of the evil eye. A dove's cry convinced Rav Ilish that a miracle would help him escape. He first listened in on the daughters and heard them say they preferred their captors over their real husbands, so he left without them. He escaped across a river, but the bird-language interpreter was caught and killed. After the daughters were later returned, Rav Ilish declared that their pot-stirring had been witchcraft, not righteousness.

people.name: Rav Ilish
people.about: captive who escapes

people.name: Rav Naḥman
people.about: his daughters are the other captives

terms.meaning: A belief that envy or too much attention can bring harm to a person.
Being held by captors, here by a foreign army or raiders.

gittin-45a-17-21.why: The mishna has just ruled that one may not help captives escape, and the Gemara asked whether that holds when there is only one captive; this tale of an escape from captivity follows.

gittin-45b-11-11.note: An Arab woman merchant brought a sack of tefillin (phylacteries, small boxes with verses worn in prayer) to Abaye. He offered one date for each pair, and in anger she threw them all into the river. Abaye then regretted it, saying he should have offered their actual value instead of speaking of them with such disrespect.

terms.meaning: Small leather boxes holding Torah verses, worn on the head and arm during morning prayer.

gittin-45b-11-11.why: The Sages have just taught that one may pay a gentile somewhat more than their value for sacred objects, up to a small coin; Abaye's lowball offer shows what is lost by paying too little.

gittin-46b-15-16.note: People from Bei Mikhsi borrowed from non-Jews, could not pay, and were seized as slaves. They asked Rav Huna to have fellow Jews redeem them, but he cited a mishna that one who sells himself to non-Jews is not redeemed. Rabbi Abba said that applies only after a repeated third time, but Rav Huna answered that these people do this habitually, so it counts as repeated. The text shows Rav Huna refusing the redemption.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: objected to Rav Huna

terms.meaning: To pay to free someone held as a slave or captive.

gittin-46b-15-16.why: The mishna rules that a man who sells himself to gentiles is not redeemed, and Rav Asi limits it to one who did so three times; this case tests that limit against people who fell into debt again and again.

gittin-46b-17-17.note: A man sold himself to gladiators and asked Rabbi Ami to redeem him. Rabbi Ami said that this should be done, since his life was at risk. The Sages said he was an apostate who ate forbidden meat. The man claimed it was only appetite, but they said he skipped permitted food for forbidden food, so Rabbi Ami told him he could not redeem him.

terms.meaning: Animals with an injury that will kill them within a year, which are forbidden to eat.
A Jew who has abandoned the religion.

gittin-46b-17-17.why: The mishna rules that a man who sells himself to gentiles is not redeemed, though his children are; Rabbi Ami argues that the danger of death should outweigh that rule, until the man's open rejection of Jewish law decides it.

gittin-47a-3-5.note: Reish Lakish sold himself to gladiators, bringing a bag with a round stone inside. He used a custom that captors grant a condemned man's last wish, asking to tie them up and strike each one. His blows killed them all and he escaped. At home, he lived without worry, saying his belly was his pillow, and left only a small measure of saffron when he died.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: a famous Talmudic sage, also called Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish

terms.meaning: Fighters who performed in arenas, here those who bought him.
A small unit of volume.

gittin-47a-3-5.why: It follows the case of an apostate who sold himself to gladiators and could not be redeemed; here a great Sage who sold himself to gladiators frees himself.

gittin-52a-12-12.note: A steward in Rabbi Meir's neighborhood was selling orphans' land to buy slaves, and Rabbi Meir did not let him. In a dream Meir was shown the words 'I wish to destroy and you build?', which could mean God wanted the orphans to lose their property. Meir ignored it, saying that words seen in dreams neither raise up nor bring down and should not be relied on.

terms.meaning: A person put in charge of an orphan's property until the child grows up.

gittin-52a-12-12.why: The teaching just quoted forbids stewards to sell orphans' fields to buy slaves, since land is the safer asset; this case shows Rabbi Meir enforcing that rule even against a dream.

gittin-52a-13-13.note: Two men, stirred up by Satan, argued every Friday at twilight. Rabbi Meir came by and stopped them three Fridays in a row until he made peace between them. He then heard Satan cry out 'Woe, Rabbi Meir has thrown me out of his house', which shows that Satan lives where there is discord.

terms.meaning: In the Talmud, a figure who tempts and stirs up trouble among people.

gittin-52a-13-13.why: The Gemara says it tells this one because it has just told another story about Rabbi Meir and a steward for orphans.

gittin-52a-14-14.note: A steward of orphans near Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi sold their land and bought oxen, and Rabbi Yehoshua said nothing against it. The Gemara explains that he agrees with Rabbi Yosei, who called his ox 'my field' because the ox is what makes a field productive. So buying oxen to work the land counts like keeping the land itself, and there was nothing to protest.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Said he never called his wife 'my wife' but 'my home', and his ox 'my field'.

terms.meaning: A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.

gittin-52a-14-14.why: The rule just taught forbids selling orphans' land to buy slaves; the Gemara explains that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi agreed with Rabbi Yosei, who called his ox 'my field', so oxen count as land.

gittin-52a-15-17.note: An old woman who cared for some orphans sold their ox, and their relatives objected to Rav Nachman. He first said that living with the orphans gave her the authority of a steward, and that a price rise after the sale was the buyer's gain, not the orphans' loss. But when the relatives pointed out that the money had not yet been paid, he agreed: orphans' property is only fully sold once money is handed over, so the orphans can raise the price or cancel the sale.

people.name: Rav Nachman
people.about: A Babylonian sage who judged this case.

people.name: Rav Chanilai bar Idi
people.about: Quoted as passing on a teaching of Shmuel.

terms.meaning: Property dedicated to the Temple, which can only be sold properly by actual payment; orphans' property is treated the same way.

gittin-52a-15-17.why: It follows a run of cases about stewards of orphans' property; this one asks who may act as steward without being appointed, and leads into Shmuel's rule on when an orphans' sale becomes final.

gittin-52a-18-18.note: Buyers agreed to buy the orphan Rabbana Ukva's wine at four dinars a barrel and took hold of it, but the price rose to six before they paid. Rav Nachman ruled that, because orphans' property is only fully acquired when money changes hands, the buyers must pay the higher price or the sale is cancelled.

people.name: Rabbana Ukva
people.about: An orphan who owned the wine.

terms.meaning: A silver coin used as money.

gittin-52a-18-18.why: It applies the rule Rav Nahman cited in the case just before; the Gemara then works out when that rule helps orphans, and Rav Sheisha objects that it could harm them.

gittin-52b-4-5.note: Orphans' relatives complained to Rav Nachman that the steward Amram the dyer dressed well and ate lavishly on the orphans' money. Rav Nachman gave innocent explanations each time: fine clothes help him be taken seriously, and perhaps he found a lost item. When they said he was actually damaging the property, Rav Nachman said to bring witnesses and he would remove him, and the Gemara concludes that a court does remove a steward who damages orphans' property.

people.name: Amram the dyer
people.about: Steward of the orphans.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: Reported a ruling in the name of Rav.

terms.meaning: Jewish law; the accepted ruling.

gittin-52b-4-5.why: The Gemara is working through the duties of a steward for orphans; this case sets the rule, disputed by the school of Rabbi Sheila, that a steward who causes loss is removed, and the Gemara rules that he is.

gittin-54a-5-5.note: Someone insulted another man by calling him a convert and the son of a convert. The man snapped back that at least he did not eat produce of the Sabbatical Year, as the insulter did. The Gemara uses this as proof that people in that place treated the Sabbatical Year ban as a serious matter, which is why Rabbi Yehuda did not impose a penalty for unintentional breaking of it.

terms.meaning: Every seventh year, when the land in Israel is left to rest and its produce is not sold or eaten in the usual way.
Someone who was not born Jewish but joined the Jewish people.

gittin-54a-5-5.why: The Gemara is explaining why Rabbi Yehuda imposed no penalty for unknowingly breaking the Sabbatical Year rules: in his place it was treated as very serious, and this exchange, where eating its produce is the worse insult, is the proof.

gittin-54b-9-9.note: A man told another: the ritually pure food I prepared with you on such and such a day became impure. The owner came before Rabbi Ami, who said that in principle the man is not believed. Rabbi Asi said to him: My teacher, do you say this? Rabbi Yohanan said in Rabbi Yosei's name: What can I do, when the Torah believed him? The text does not say how Rabbi Ami responded.
gittin-54b-9-9.why: A teaching just quoted says a helper is believed that food became impure while he is still working on it, but not about a past day; Rabbi Asi's report challenges that, and the Gemara next asks where the Torah believes such a person.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Sage who ruled that the man is not believed about the past.

people.name: Rabbi Asi
people.about: Challenged Rabbi Ami, citing Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Reported Rabbi Yosei's saying that the Torah believes such a person.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Sage who said, What can I do, when the Torah believed him?

terms.meaning: Food kept free of ritual impurity, a religious status that contact with certain things can transfer. Impure food could not be eaten by those keeping these rules.

gittin-54b-13-14.note: A scribe told Rabbi Ami that he had not written God's names with the proper intention in a Torah scroll he made for a buyer, which would make it invalid. Rabbi Ami ruled that he is believed enough to lose his payment, but not believed enough to disqualify the scroll the buyer holds. Rabbi Yirmeya asked whether he loses payment for the whole scroll or just the God's names; Rabbi Ami said the whole scroll, since a scroll with those names written wrongly is worth nothing.

terms.meaning: The requirement that a scribe have in mind that he is writing a holy name when he writes it.

gittin-54b-13-14.why: The Gemara is asking when a person is believed about past work he did for others; next it asks why the scribe was not told to go over the names again, and whose opinion that follows.

gittin-54b-18-18.note: A scribe came before Rabbi Abbahu and said that he had not prepared the parchment of a Torah scroll he wrote for a client with the proper intention. Rabbi Abbahu asked who had the scroll; the buyer did. Rabbi Abbahu said: since you are believed to lose your wage, you are believed to make the Torah scroll unfit.
gittin-54b-18-18.why: It contrasts with Rabbi Ami's ruling just before; the Gemara explains that Rabbi Ami's scribe may have lied, thinking he would lose only part of his pay, while this scribe knew he was giving up his entire wage, so he is believed.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: Sage who ruled that the scribe's confession disqualifies the scroll.

terms.meaning: Animal skin prepared for writing. For a Torah scroll it must be processed with the intention that it is for that holy use.

gittin-55b-6-6.note: Rava objects, using a mishna and a baraita (an early teaching outside the mishna), that a thief who consecrates a stolen animal is still liable for karet, a severe heavenly punishment. That seems to need the thief to own it. Rav Sheizevi's answer made people laugh, but Rava defends it: the Sages themselves made the thief's consecration valid, so the animal counts as his.

terms.meaning: A severe punishment of being cut off from the Jewish people, imposed by Heaven.
To set an animal aside as holy, as an offering.
An early teaching not included in the Mishna.

gittin-55b-6-6.why: The Gemara is weighing Ulla's and Rav Yehuda's views on whether the Sages made a stolen offering valid or invalid; Rava's objection tests whether an owner's despair alone lets a thief acquire what he stole.

gittin-55b-15-17.note: Rabbi Yochanan says Jerusalem fell because of Kamtza and bar Kamtza. A host mistakenly invited his enemy bar Kamtza to a feast and threw him out despite offers to pay. Angry that the Sages stayed silent, bar Kamtza told the Roman emperor the Jews were rebelling, and tricked them by blemishing an offering he brought. Rabbi Zekharya ben Avkolas blocked every fix the Sages proposed, and the war with Rome began.

people.name: Bar Kamtza
people.about: the host's enemy, mistakenly invited

terms.meaning: A physical defect that makes an animal unfit to be offered on the altar.
The central holy building in Jerusalem, where offerings were brought.

gittin-55b-15-17.why: The mishna's law of Sicarii is tied to the war against Rome, and the Gemara now turns to how that war and the destruction of the Temple began, opening with a verse about one who hardens his heart.

gittin-56a-5-6.note: Rome sent Nero against the Jews. He shot arrows in all four directions and each one landed in Jerusalem. Then he asked a child to recite a verse he had learned, and it was 'I will lay My vengeance upon Edom by the hand of My people Israel'. Nero concluded that God wanted to destroy the Temple and then punish him for it, so he fled and became a convert, and Rabbi Meir was said to be his descendant.

people.name: Nero Caesar
people.about: Roman emperor.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: Said here to descend from Nero.

terms.meaning: The descendants of Esau; the Talmud uses it as a name for Rome.

gittin-56a-5-6.why: It continues the Gemara's account of the war that destroyed the Second Temple, which began with bar Kamtza's slander; the Roman response comes in stages, and Nero is the first general sent.

gittin-56a-7-9.note: Vespasian besieged Jerusalem for three years. Three rich men, Nakdimon ben Guryon, ben Kalba Savua and ben Tzitzit HaKesat, offered food, drink and firewood, enough for twenty-one years. The Sages wanted to make peace with Rome, but the zealots refused and wanted to fight. To force the issue, the zealots burned the storehouses of wheat and barley, and a famine followed.

people.name: Vespasian
people.about: Roman general who besieged Jerusalem.

people.name: Nakdimon ben Guryon
people.about: One of three wealthy men of Jerusalem.

people.name: Rav Chisda
people.about: Quoted on how costly firewood is.

terms.meaning: Hardline fighters in besieged Jerusalem who opposed making peace with Rome.

gittin-56a-7-9.why: It continues the Gemara's account of the war that ended in the destruction of the Temple, moving from Nero to Vespasian's siege.

gittin-56a-10-13.note: During the famine, the rich woman Marta bat Baitos sent her agent for flour, but each kind (fine, ordinary, coarse, even barley) was sold out before he got there. She went out to look for food herself, stepped on dung, and died of disgust. Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai applied to her a verse about a tender and delicate woman. Another version says she died of disgust after eating a fig that Rabbi Tzadok had sucked dry. He ate figs this way while breaking the fasts he kept for forty years, praying that Jerusalem would not be destroyed. It is also told that as she was dying she threw her gold and silver into the marketplace, saying she had no use for it, which the Gemara links to a verse in Ezekiel.

people.name: Marta bat Baitos
people.about: A wealthy woman of Jerusalem.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Fasted forty years, praying Jerusalem would not be destroyed.

terms.meaning: Fine flour, the best kind.

gittin-56a-10-13.why: The zealots have just burned the city's food stores and brought famine; this story shows what that famine did, even to the richest of Jerusalem.

gittin-56a-14-17.note: Abba Sikkara, leader of Jerusalem's zealots and nephew of Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai, came to him in secret. Rabban Yoḥanan asked how long they would kill everyone by starvation; Abba Sikkara said the zealots would kill him if he spoke out, and told him to fake illness and death and be carried out. Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua carried him, and at the gate Abba Sikkara stopped the guards from piercing or pushing him. In the Roman camp he hailed Vespasian as king, citing verses, but fell silent at Vespasian's parable of a snake around a barrel of honey. When a messenger announced Vespasian would be emperor and his shoe would not go on, Rabban Yoḥanan explained why and how to fix it.
gittin-56a-14-17.why: The Gemara is telling the story of the siege and fall of Jerusalem; just before this, the wealthy Marta bat Baitos dies in the same famine Rabban Yoḥanan blames on the zealots.

people.name: Abba Sikkara
people.about: Leader of the zealots of Jerusalem and nephew of Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai

people.name: Rabban Yoḥanan ben Zakkai
people.about: A leading Sage who escapes the besieged city to meet the Roman commander

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: One of the students who carry him out of the city

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: The other student who carries him out

people.name: Vespasian
people.about: The Roman commander besieging Jerusalem, who is named emperor

terms.meaning: Armed rebels inside besieged Jerusalem who refused any peace with Rome.
The holy sanctuary in Jerusalem, center of Jewish worship, which the Romans destroyed.

gittin-56b-7-16.note: Titus conquered the Temple, brought a prostitute into the Holy of Holies, did a shameful act on a Torah scroll, and slashed the curtain, which poured out blood. He also loaded the sacred vessels onto a ship to be praised in his city for conquering Jerusalem. At sea a wave nearly drowned him, and he boasted that God only had power over water. A heavenly voice dared him to go up on dry land and fight a gnat; when he did, a gnat entered his nose and ate at his brain for seven years. Hammering eased it for thirty days. When he was dying he ordered that he be burned and his ashes scattered across the seven seas so God could not find him and judge him. After his death his head was opened and the gnat was found to be the size of a sparrow.

people.name: Titus
people.about: Roman commander who took Jerusalem; son of Vespasian.

people.name: Rabbi Pinchas ben Arova
people.about: Said he was in Rome when Titus died and saw the gnat.

terms.meaning: The innermost room of the Temple, which only the High Priest entered, once a year.
A teaching from the time of the Mishnah that was not included in the Mishnah itself.

gittin-56b-7-16.why: It continues the Gemara's account of the destruction: after Vespasian leaves for Rome, Titus completes the conquest, and the Gemara tells how he desecrated the Temple and how he was punished.

gittin-56b-17-17.note: Onkelos bar Kalonikos, Titus's nephew, wanted to convert. He raised Titus from the dead by necromancy and asked who matters most in that world. Titus said the Jewish people, but told him their commandments were too many to keep and he should fight them instead; asked his own punishment, Titus said his ashes are gathered, judged, burned and scattered over the seven seas every day. Onkelos raised Balaam, who told him not to seek their peace, and is punished in boiling semen. Then he raised Jesus the Nazarene, who told him to seek their welfare, and is punished in boiling excrement. The Gemara draws the contrast between the sinners of Israel and the prophets of the nations. The text here does not say what Onkelos then did.
gittin-56b-17-17.why: The Gemara has just told of Titus's death and his order that his ashes be scattered so the God of the Jews could not judge him; here that very sentence is carried out on him every day.

people.name: Onkelos bar Kalonikos
people.about: Titus's sister's son, who wants to convert to Judaism

people.name: Titus
people.about: The Roman who destroyed the Temple, raised from the dead by Onkelos

people.name: Balaam
people.about: The gentile prophet of the Bible who wished Israel harm, raised by Onkelos

people.name: Jesus the Nazarene
people.about: Raised by Onkelos; the Gemara calls him a sinner of Israel who sought their welfare

terms.meaning: Calling up the spirit of a dead person to speak with them.
To become Jewish by formally accepting the Torah and its commandments.

gittin-57a-4-8.note: At the King's Mountain it was the custom to carry a rooster and a hen before a bride and groom. One day Roman soldiers took them, the people beat the soldiers, and the soldiers told the emperor the Jews had rebelled. He attacked. Bar Deroma, who could leap a mil, killed many Romans, until he quoted a psalm as a complaint against God; then a snake eviscerated him in an outhouse and he died. The emperor withdrew, but when the Jews celebrated with lamps, he said they were rejoicing over him and returned. Rav Asi says three hundred thousand swordsmen massacred the people for three days and nights while weddings went on at the other side, neither knowing of the other.
gittin-57a-4-8.why: The Gemara is recounting disasters of the war with Rome; it said earlier that the King's Mountain was destroyed over a rooster and a hen, and after the story of Kamtza and bar Kamtza it now gives the details.

people.name: bar Deroma
people.about: A man of the King's Mountain who could leap a mil and killed many Romans

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The Sage who reports the size of the massacre

terms.meaning: Tur Malka, a large, heavily populated region of the Land of Israel.
A unit of distance, roughly a kilometer.

gittin-57a-14-15.note: Three Sages were sitting together and asked whether anyone had heard anything about the town of Kefar Sekhanya. One of them told of a betrothed man and woman who were taken captive, and their captors married them to each other. She said to him: Please do not touch me, as I have no marriage contract from you. He did not touch her until the day he died. When he died, she told the Sages to eulogize him as a man who conquered his passion more than Joseph: Joseph was tested for a short time, not in one bed, and not with his own wife, while this man was tested every day, in one bed, with his own wife.
gittin-57a-14-15.why: The Gemara is speaking of the towns of the King's Mountain region and how they were destroyed; three Sages share what they heard of one such town, and this is the first account.

people.name: Joseph
people.about: The biblical figure who resisted Potiphar's wife; the woman compares her husband to him.

terms.meaning: In Jewish law, the first stage of marriage: the couple are legally bound but do not yet live together.
The ketubba, the document that secures a wife's financial rights; the woman holds that they may not live together without one.

gittin-57a-17-18.note: A husband wanted to divorce his wife without paying her large marriage contract. He got his friends drunk, put them in bed with her, smeared egg white to look like evidence, and brought witnesses to court claiming adultery. Bava ben Buta, a student of Shammai, said that egg white hardens near fire while semen is absorbed. They tested it, found egg white, and punished the husband with lashes and made him pay her contract in full.

people.name: Bava ben Buta
people.about: A disciple of Shammai the Elder.

terms.meaning: A document in which a husband commits to pay his wife a set sum if he divorces her or dies.

gittin-57a-17-18.why: Three Sages are telling what they know of the town of Kefar Sekhanya in the King's Mountain region; after the discussion Abaye asks why such righteous people were destroyed.

gittin-57b-11-12.note: Four hundred boys and girls were taken captive to be used for prostitution. They asked whether drowning themselves in the sea would still bring them to the World-to-Come, and the eldest cited a verse that God will bring back those who drown for Heaven's sake. The girls jumped into the sea, and the boys reasoned that if the girls would do it, they should too, and followed. The passage applies the verse about being killed all day long to them.

terms.meaning: The afterlife, where the righteous receive their reward.

gittin-57b-11-12.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of the calamities that befell Israel in the destruction; this one ends with a verse, and the next account applies the same verse to another case of martyrdom.

gittin-57b-13-19.note: A woman's seven sons were brought one by one before the emperor and told to worship an idol. Each refused, quoting a Torah verse, and each was killed. The youngest was offered a trick to save his life, dropping the emperor's seal and picking it up, but he refused too, saying that if he should honor Caesar, he must all the more honor God. His mother kissed him goodbye, said she had bound seven altars, then fell from a roof and died. A heavenly voice called her a joyful mother of children.

people.name: The mother and her seven sons
people.about: Unnamed in the text.

people.name: Abraham
people.about: Whom the mother mentions, since he bound one son (Isaac) on an altar.

terms.meaning: Dying rather than break the Torah's core commandments, as a witness to God.

gittin-57b-13-19.why: The children who drowned themselves were tied to the verse For Your sake we are killed all the day long; Rav Yehuda says the verse refers to this woman and her seven sons.

gittin-58a-5-5.note: The Gemara describes the cruel treatment of handsome Jewish children by Roman nobles after the Great Revolt. In one case two of the children talk. One asks where such suffering appears in the Torah, and the other cites a verse about plagues not written in the Torah. When the first asks how far off in his studies that verse was, his friend says one and a half columns. He answers that he would not have needed him.

terms.meaning: The Jewish war against Rome that ended with the destruction of the Temple.

gittin-58a-5-5.why: The Gemara has just read the precious sons of Zion, comparable to fine gold, as describing children so beautiful they put fine gold to shame; this shows what their beauty brought on them.

gittin-58a-7-7.note: Rav Yehuda quotes Shmuel, who quotes Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, to explain a verse from Lamentations. The city of Beitar had four hundred synagogues, each with four hundred teachers and four hundred pupils. When the enemy broke in, the children attacked with their pens. After the enemy won, they wrapped the children in their scrolls and burned them.
gittin-58a-7-7.why: It explains a verse from Lamentations, My eye affects my soul because of all the daughters of my city, as part of the Gemara's run of accounts of what happened to Jewish children in the destruction.

gittin-58a-8-9.note: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Chananya came to Rome and heard of a handsome child in prison. Standing outside, he quoted a verse about Israel being given to robbers, and the child finished it correctly, with the reason, that we sinned against God. Rabbi Yehoshua was sure the child would become a great teacher and swore not to leave until he ransomed him. He paid a great sum, and soon the child was giving legal rulings in Israel. He was Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
people.about: The child who was ransomed.

terms.meaning: Decisions on what Jewish law requires.

gittin-58a-8-9.why: The Gemara is gathering accounts of what became of Jewish children in the destruction; this one is introduced as another teaching about their fate.

gittin-58a-10-12.note: The son and daughter of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha the High Priest were captured and sold to two different masters. The masters decided to pair the two beautiful slaves and share the children, and locked them in a room. Each sat in a corner and wept, unwilling to marry a slave given their priestly descent. At dawn they recognized each other as brother and sister and died of grief, and the passage connects their fate with Jeremiah's lament.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha
people.about: Called the High Priest here; his son and daughter are the subjects.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports this in the name of Rav.

terms.meaning: A descendant of Aaron, with special status and marriage restrictions.

gittin-58a-10-12.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha himself was ransomed as a child from captivity in Rome; this follows with what happened to his own son and daughter.

gittin-58a-13-15.note: Reish Lakish tells of Tzafenat bat Peniel, a High Priest's daughter known for her beauty. After she was captured and abused, she was put up for sale in seven garments, and an ugly man insisted on seeing her beauty. Six garments were removed, and she tore the seventh herself and rolled in ashes. She cried out to God, asking why He had not shown pity at least for the sake of His own holy name by which they are called.

people.name: Tzafenat bat Peniel
people.about: A High Priest's daughter known for her beauty.

gittin-58a-13-15.why: It is one in a run of accounts of the children of priestly families taken captive in the destruction, following the story of Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha's son and daughter.

gittin-58a-17-20.note: A carpenter's apprentice wanted his master's wife. He kept her for three days when she came to get a loan, then falsely told the master she had been attacked on the way back. He persuaded the master to divorce her, lent him money for her marriage contract, and married her himself. When the master could not repay, the apprentice made him work it off, serving the couple their drinks with tears falling into the cups. The Gemara says Israel's sentence was sealed for staying silent about this, though some say it was for the couple's earlier adultery.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Reports this in the name of Rav.

terms.meaning: A document in which a husband commits to pay his wife a set sum if he divorces her or dies.

gittin-58a-17-20.why: Rav Yehuda tells it to explain the verse So they oppress a man and his house, as a last account of the sins and sorrows of the destruction before the Gemara returns to the mishna's law of Sicarii.

gittin-58b-9-10.note: Giddel bar Re'ilai took over land in a valley in return for paying its land tax, and paid three years in advance. After the first year the original owners came back and said: you have eaten the produce for the year you paid; now we will pay and we will eat. The case came before Rav Pappa, who thought to give Giddel a document letting him claim the land from the valley's residents. Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua, objected that this would treat the case like that of a Sicarius. Instead he ruled that Giddel had put his money on the horn of a deer: he had risked it himself and could not claim it back.
gittin-58b-9-10.why: Rav Yosef has just said the law of unjust seizure is not applied in Babylonia, since owners there can complain to the government; this case tests how far that reaches.

people.name: Giddel bar Re'ilai
people.about: A man who paid three years' land tax in advance in return for using the land.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The judge before whom the case was brought.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Yehoshua
people.about: A Sage who objects to Rav Pappa's plan and rules against Giddel.

terms.meaning: In this discussion, someone who seized land by violence or threats; the Sages set special rules for buying land from such a person.
A tax owed by the residents of the valley on their land, paid jointly.

terms.term: on the horn of a deer
terms.meaning: A saying for money put somewhere it can run off: Giddel risked it by paying in advance.

gittin-60b-13-14.note: Rav Shimi bar Ashi wants to study with Abaye, but Abaye is busy irrigating his fields. Rav Shimi offers to irrigate by day so they can learn at night. He then tells the upper-field owners that the lower fields drink first (Rav's view) and the lower-field owners the opposite (Shmuel's view), and while they argue he dams the river and waters Abaye's fields. Abaye points out he acted on two opposing opinions, and refused to eat that year's produce, fearing the water came unlawfully.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: the Sage whose fields needed water

people.name: Rav
people.about: cited for one view on who drinks first

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: cited for the opposing view
